analysis.investment_thesis: Afcons is a seasoned infrastructure EPC contractor with international project execution capability, but its financials display almost every characteristic Fisher avoids: sub-5% revenue CAGR, revenue contraction in FY25, negative operating cash flow in FY25, high finance costs (INR 629 Cr on INR 12,548 Cr revenue = 5% interest burden), and ROE of only 11.1%. This is a cyclical government-order-dependent business, not a compounding growth machine.
key_strengths: ROCE of 19.6% approaches Fisher's threshold and reflects genuine project execution efficiency on a large asset base
Diversified project portfolio across marine, metro, tunnels, and oil & gas globally — reduces concentration in any single sector or geography
Net profit CAGR of 14.4% over five years, with reserves growing from INR 1,721 Cr to INR 5,021 Cr — equity value has been built
key_risks: Revenue of INR 12,548 Cr in FY25 is below FY24's INR 13,268 Cr and barely above FY23's INR 12,637 Cr — the growth story has stalled
Finance costs of INR 629 Cr in FY25 (a 10% CAGR over five years) eat deeply into thin operating margins of 10.65%; interest coverage is uncomfortably low
OCF turned negative (-INR 132 Cr) in FY25 for the first time — working capital deterioration in a capital-intensive EPC business is a serious warning
red_flags: Free cash flow of -INR 470 Cr in FY25 — the worst in five years — signals simultaneous deterioration in operations and heavy capex with no near-term FCF visibility
'Other income' of INR 469 Cr in FY25 is nearly as large as operating profit of INR 1,361 Cr, suggesting reported net profit is substantially dependent on non-operating items
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Afcons possesses genuine project execution capability in technically complex infrastructure — offshore marine, underground metro, and high-altitude tunnels are not businesses any contractor can enter. However, the business model is fundamentally order-book driven: revenue recognition depends on project award cycles, government capital expenditure budgets, and execution timelines, all of which create violent earnings cyclicality. The five-year revenue CAGR of 4.8% is simply incompatible with Fisher's growth criteria, and FY25's revenue decline and negative OCF make the near-term picture worse, not better.

The valuation at P/E 24x and EV/EBITDA 10.7x appears optically modest, but Fisher does not buy cheap businesses — he buys great businesses. The ROE of 11.1% on a heavily leveraged balance sheet (D/E 0.66, borrowings INR 3,565 Cr) means shareholders are not being adequately compensated for the capital deployed. Until revenue growth re-accelerates above 15% and OCF consistently covers capex, this does not meet the Fisher standard.
